analysis.one_liner: Repeals the recent corporate tax cuts and forgives all federal student loans, with half the savings boosting Pell Grants.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the 2017 tax law and cancel every federal student loan drew 20 House sponsors and cosponsors, all Democrats, and died in committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have erased the entire 2017 tax-cut law (the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act), putting tax rules back to what they were before it, and used the added revenue to cancel the full balance — principal and interest — of every federal student loan, tax-free. Half of any leftover savings would go to raising the maximum Pell Grant for ten years and the other half to reducing the deficit. It never advanced past committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Every borrower with a federal student loan would have had their entire remaining balance forgiven within 180 days, tax-free — the bill covers loans made, insured, or guaranteed under the federal student loan programs [S3]. Low-income students would gain from a decade of increases to the maximum Pell Grant, protected as mandatory spending so future Congresses couldn't cut it without changing the law [S3]. The CRS summary confirms the bill terminates the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act and forgives outstanding federal student loans [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Federal student loan borrowers and Pell students

how_it_helps.text: Forgives the full outstanding principal and interest on all eligible federal student loans within 180 days of enactment, and makes sure the forgiven amount is not taxed as income to the borrower

Rolls back the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act entirely — the bill applies the tax code as if that law had never been enacted — which would restore the pre-2017 corporate tax rate and taxes on high earners
Directs half the net savings to raise the maximum Pell Grant for ten straight award years and locks in that higher level permanently; the other half goes to deficit reduction

analysis.who_pays: Corporations and high-income households would bear the largest cost, since repealing the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act would restore the pre-2017 corporate rate, top individual rates, and estate-tax rules [S2][S3]. Because that law also cut rates for most middle-income filers, a full repeal would raise taxes on many ordinary households as well. The federal Treasury would absorb the cost of wiping out the loans, which the bill intends to offset with the restored tax revenue [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Corporations, wealthy households, and middle-class taxpayers

drawbacks.text: A blanket wipeout of all federal student debt is poorly targeted: a surgeon and a struggling dropout with the same balance get the same benefit, and people who already repaid their loans get nothing
Repealing the entire 2017 tax law would raise taxes on many middle-income families, not just corporations and the wealthy, because that law cut individual rates across income levels
Canceling everyone's balance at once gives colleges no reason to rein in tuition, and could leave future borrowers facing the same debt spiral with no relief

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is enormous and concrete: total debt freedom for tens of millions of borrowers and a bigger, locked-in Pell Grant for low-income students. The downside is real too — the bill pays for it by reversing the entire 2017 tax law, which would raise taxes on many middle-class families along with corporations and the wealthy, and the one-time forgiveness does nothing for future students or for people who already paid off their loans. A narrower bill that repealed only the corporate and top-rate cuts, or forgave debt on a sliding scale, would have been better designed.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to four House committees and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the two-year Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Jared Polis introduced the bill on May 23, 2018, joined by 11 original co-sponsors including Reps. Ellison, DeLauro, Jayapal, and Maloney
The House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee plus the Education and the Workforce, Natural Resources, and Energy and Commerce Committees on the day of introduction
In June and October 2018 it was passed down to subcommittees on energy and mineral resources and on higher education, and no further action ever followed
The bill finished with 19 cosponsors, all Democrats, and the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 with the bill still sitting in committee

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporations and high-income households came out ahead: the 2017 tax cuts stayed in place, and no student borrower received any relief.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Corporations and wealthy households kept the tax cuts

sides.party_line_note: All 20 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; not a single Republican signed on, and the chamber never voted.

industries.note: Repealing the 2017 tax law would have restored the 35% corporate tax rate the law cut to 21%, plus the provisions corporations use to lower their bills. The bill's core premise is that corporate tax savings should be redirected to student debt relief instead.

industries.industry: Student loan servicers and FFEL lenders
industries.note: Forgiving every federal loan — including privately held guaranteed loans — would have ended the steady interest and servicing revenue these companies collect from borrowers, much of it from people who will repay far more than they borrowed.

Full repeal would have restored the higher top individual rates, limited the pass-through deduction, and revived the larger estate tax, reversing the provisions of the 2017 law that flowed most heavily to the wealthiest households.
A decade of automatic maximum Pell Grant increases would have put more federal aid dollars on campus, though the one-time debt wipeout gives schools no incentive to slow tuition growth.
